Scoping Review Finds Artificial Intelligence Tools Boost Early Language Learning in Children

A comprehensive scoping review published in the journal AI, Brain and Child demonstrates that artificial intelligence technologies can significantly enhance early language and literacy development among children aged three to eight years old. Conducted by researchers He Sun, Justina Tan, and Ming Chong Lim, the investigation systematically examined how computational tools personalize instructional input during formative developmental periods. Acquiring foundational language skills in early childhood establishes the essential bedrock for subsequent academic achievement and long-term success. However, young learners routinely face systemic bottlenecks within primary learning environments. In home settings, socioeconomic disparities and variable language practices create significant inequities in the quality and frequency of caregiver interactions. Meanwhile, formal classrooms frequently rely on teacher-centered, one-size-fits-all instruction that contradicts developmental recommendations for child-centered learning. The authors found that artificial intelligence tools effectively bridge these institutional gaps by delivering tailored instruction and responsive feedback, yielding developmental gains that consistently match or significantly exceed traditional educational methods across diverse early learning settings.

To map the nascent landscape of artificial intelligence in early language education, the researchers implemented the five-stage scoping review framework established by Arksey and O’Malley, adhering to PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. The inquiry formulated five specific research questions to identify prevalent computational tools, examine their theoretical foundations, evaluate experimental effectiveness, analyze moderating intervention variables, and document common methodological limitations. A systematic literature search was executed across six academic databases: PsycINFO, Academic Search Complete, Computer Source via EBSCOhost, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, the Education Database, and EBSCOHost ERIC. The initial automated search identified 1,296 candidate records. The resulting 70 eligible publications underwent full-text assessment against explicit criteria requiring empirical AI interventions, standardized linguistic measures, and participant age ranges between three and eight years old. Ultimately, twelve peer-reviewed experimental articles published through 2021 met all inclusion standards.

The twelve synthesized investigations reflected a notable geographic concentration in Western nations while incorporating participants from nine distinct countries or regions. Eight studies took place within Western environments, including three in the United States and five across Europe, specifically Italy, the Netherlands, France, Spain, and Germany. East Asian settings contributed two studies, conducted in the Republic of Korea and Taiwan, while two additional investigations occurred in Iran within the Middle East. Participant cohorts comprised monolingual children, bilingual learners, and English language learners. To verify evidence quality, the authors conducted a formal risk-of-bias evaluation using the ROBINS-I tool across seven core domains: confounding, participant selection, intervention classification, deviations from intended protocols, missing data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting. The evaluation confirmed a low to moderate risk of confounding bias across all twelve studies, with researchers appropriately controlling for baseline age and language background. Low risk ratings were consistently documented across participant classification, objective outcome measurement, and reporting integrity.

Regarding technological systems, social robots represented the predominant instructional medium, appearing in nine of the twelve studies, with eight relying on robots exclusively. The autonomous humanoid NAO robot was the most frequently studied platform across four papers, featuring anthropomorphic physical structures, facial articulation, gestures, simulated breathing motions, and adaptable tutoring algorithms. Three investigations utilized the Tega robot, an autonomous platform featuring a plush exterior, child-friendly vocal acoustics, and expressive multi-axis facial animatronics designed to elicit positive affect. Less common robotic platforms, such as the Julia robot, utilized articulated mechanical arms to display affective responsiveness. The remaining four studies evaluated alternative digital technologies for early language instruction. These comprised an interactive hologram system developed by Cerezo and colleagues to teach spoken pronunciation, a kinesthetic motion-sensing platform called En Plein studied by Goffredo and colleagues that mapped bodily movements onto screen avatars, and the Kaligo digital tablet application evaluated by Bonneton-Botté and colleagues to train handwriting.

The pedagogical architecture of these computational interventions grounded itself in developmental psychology, educational theory, and human-computer interaction. Qualitative coding of theoretical concepts revealed three central frameworks guiding system design. First, 42 percent of the articles explicitly adopted Lev Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development, implementing scaffolding frameworks that adapt instructional difficulty to a learner’s evolving mastery. Computational models such as adaptive Bayesian Knowledge Tracing operationalized this scaffolding by continually evaluating child competence and introducing advanced tasks following lower-level mastery. Second, 42 percent of the studies emphasized anthropomorphic attributes within human-computer and human-robot interaction frameworks, arguing that physical embodiment, verbal responsiveness, and nonverbal gesturing optimize communicative reciprocity between young learners and machines. Third, 33 percent of the studies applied Albert Bandura’s social learning theory, leveraging speech-to-text algorithms, vocal imitation, and visual modeling to support language acquisition through observation, as demonstrated in robotic pronunciation guidance and handwriting motion tracing.

Direct empirical evidence regarding instructional effectiveness was established by eight studies that evaluated artificial intelligence interventions against non-AI control groups utilizing traditional pedagogical approaches. In six of those eight studies, representing 75 percent of comparative trials, children in the artificial intelligence condition achieved statistically significant learning advantages over control participants. In one study by Yueh and colleagues assessing reading comprehension in Mandarin Chinese, children reading alongside the Julia robot companion performed comparably to those reading with human tutors, establishing educational equivalence without compromising student outcomes. Another investigation by Goffredo and colleagues reported descriptive improvements in phonological awareness through the En Plein motion-sensing system compared to standard classes, though inferential statistical significance was not evaluated. Synthesizing these comparative findings, artificial intelligence proved statistically effective in 87.5 percent of evaluated studies, while descriptive evaluations indicated instructional benefits across all eight comparative investigations, establishing that computational interventions consistently equaled or surpassed conventional human-led instructional methods.

The scoping analysis examined whether the instructional language or the computational architecture moderated overall intervention effectiveness.
